chapters.title: Chapter 5: Building a Forward-Looking Investment Framework

lessons.title: Scenario Planning: Fragmentation, Reglobalization or Bifurcation into Blocs

children.text: In the early 1970s, planners at Royal Dutch Shell, led by Pierre Wack, made an unusual choice. Instead of producing a single forecast for the price of oil, they built several distinct, internally consistent stories about how the oil market could evolve, including one where an oil-producing cartel deliberately restricted supply. When the 1973 OPEC embargo hit, Shell's management had already mentally rehearsed that exact scenario, and the company navigated the shock more effectively than rivals who had bet everything on a single forecast. That is the discipline this final lesson borrows. After four chapters of facts and case studies, the honest next step is not a prediction, it is a small set of scenarios worth actually planning around.

body.text: Nobody can reliably predict which single path global trade takes from here. What you can do is build a small number of genuinely distinct scenarios, identify the indicators that would tell you which one is unfolding, and position a portfolio so it survives being wrong about which one wins.

children.text: Three Scenarios for Where This Goes

Every trend documented across this course, tariffs, export controls, friendshoring, critical mineral leverage, points in a consistent direction. But direction is not destination, and three genuinely different destinations remain plausible.

body.caption: Three scenarios for the global trade order
headers: What would confirm it is unfolding

cells: The current trajectory continues: gradual friendshoring, managed decoupling in strategic sectors like chips and critical minerals, while broad consumer trade keeps flowing relatively freely
Steady, incremental tariff and export control announcements; continued China+1 corporate diversification; no major crisis, no major thaw
Major powers step back from escalation, driven by economic cost fatigue, leadership change, or a renewed diplomatic effort
Meaningful tariff rollbacks; eased export controls; resumed high-level US-China dialogue producing concrete agreements, not just meetings; WTO reform gaining real traction
A major crisis, such as a serious Taiwan Strait escalation, accelerates a split into largely separate US-aligned and China-aligned economic and technology spheres
Sharp acceleration in export controls and sanctions; countries pressured to choose sides explicitly; sustained military escalation signals; collapse of remaining multilateral trade forums

body.text: Most professional forecasters and institutional strategists currently treat continued fragmentation, the middle scenario, as the base case, with reglobalization and hard bifurcation as the two tail scenarios on either side. That consensus itself is a data point worth tracking, not a certainty, and it can shift quickly if the confirming indicators for either tail scenario start showing up.

children.text: Where India Sits Across All Three

India's foreign policy posture, often described by Indian officials as multi-alignment rather than the older non-alignment of the Cold War era, means engaging the Quad with the US, Japan and Australia while simultaneously remaining active in the China and Russia-linked SCO and BRICS groupings. This positions India with real optionality across all three scenarios this lesson describes, though not equal comfort in each.
India keeps benefiting from friendshoring exactly as Chapters 3 and 4 documented, while continuing to manage its own dependencies on Chinese capital goods and components.

India benefits too, through freer trade access and lower input costs, but loses some of the specific competitive edge it has gained from Western companies actively avoiding China, since that pressure eases.

This is the scenario that tests multi-alignment hardest. A genuine forced choice between blocs would be far more disruptive to India's current strategy than either of the other two scenarios, since much of its present advantage comes precisely from not having to choose.
A Monitoring Checklist Across All Five Chapters

body.title: Indicators to watch, drawn from this entire course
steps: Freight rates, PMI new orders and inventory-to-sales ratios, the Chapter 2 leading indicators, for early signs of stress in either direction
The outcome of the USMCA joint review, a dated, concrete test of whether nearshoring rules tighten or loosen
China's rare earth, gallium, germanium and graphite export control announcements, as a real-time gauge of escalation or restraint
Frequency and substance of high-level US-China dialogue, watching for actual agreements rather than just meetings taking place
India's own trade deficit with China and its crude oil and semiconductor import dependence, to track whether its structural vulnerabilities are actually narrowing
Military and diplomatic signals around Taiwan specifically, given how directly Chapter 3 tied a severe disruption there to the hard bifurcation scenario

body.title: Position a portfolio across scenarios
body.scenario: You manage a portfolio with meaningful exposure to Indian electronics manufacturing services, Indian specialty chemicals exporters, and Indian IT services companies serving US and European clients.
body.prompt: For each of the three scenarios in this lesson, briefly describe whether that portfolio mix is likely to be a relative winner, a relative loser, or roughly neutral, and explain the one biggest risk you would want to hedge against if you believed hard bifurcation was becoming more likely.
body.modelAnswer: Under continued fragmentation, the base case, this mix should perform reasonably well, since electronics manufacturing services and specialty chemicals both directly benefit from ongoing China+1 diversification, while IT services grows more slowly but steadily. Under reglobalization, IT services likely benefits from renewed global growth and capital spending, while the diversification-driven tailwind for electronics and chemicals partially fades as the urgency behind China+1 eases. Under hard bifurcation, all three face real risk: electronics manufacturing services is exposed through its continued reliance on imported components and chips, specialty chemicals could face disrupted input supply chains of its own, and IT services would be hit hardest of all by a serious global recession or a forced-alignment scenario that disrupted its Western client relationships. If hard bifurcation looked increasingly likely, the biggest single risk to hedge would be a sharp cut to Western corporate technology and discretionary spending, which would hit IT services directly and quickly, exactly the destocking and demand-cut dynamic covered in Chapter 2's supply chain stress lesson, just applied to services rather than goods.

body.title: Test the scenario discipline
body.question: According to this lesson's framing of Shell's 1970s scenario planning, what was the actual advantage of building multiple scenarios rather than one best forecast?
options: It guaranteed Shell would predict the exact oil price correctly
It let Shell's management mentally rehearse a disruptive scenario in advance, so they reacted faster and more effectively when something similar actually happened
It eliminated the need for any further monitoring of oil markets
It was primarily a public relations exercise with no real decision-making value
body.explanation: Scenario planning's value is not predictive accuracy, it is preparedness. Shell did not know the 1973 embargo would happen, but having already reasoned through a similar scenario meant the organisation could recognise and respond to it faster than competitors who had never considered the possibility at all.

cards.definition: A strategic planning method, pioneered at scale by Royal Dutch Shell in the 1970s, that builds several distinct, internally consistent future scenarios rather than relying on a single point forecast.
The base case is the outcome considered most likely by current consensus; tail scenarios are less likely but still plausible outcomes on either side of it, each worth its own contingency planning.

India's current foreign policy posture of actively engaging multiple, sometimes opposing geopolitical groupings simultaneously, such as the Quad and BRICS, distinct from the passive non-alignment of the Cold War era.

points: Scenario planning, pioneered by Shell in the 1970s, beats single-point forecasting for genuinely uncertain, high-stakes questions like the future of global trade, because it builds preparedness rather than false precision.
Continued fragmentation is the current consensus base case, with reglobalization and hard bifurcation into blocs as the two tail scenarios worth planning around, not ignoring.
India's multi-alignment strategy gives it real optionality across all three scenarios, but hard bifurcation is specifically the scenario that would force the hardest, most disruptive choices.

A concrete, course-wide monitoring checklist, freight rates and PMI data, the USMCA review outcome, China's mineral export controls, and Taiwan-specific signals, turns abstract scenario planning into an actionable habit.

The right question when building a portfolio is never "which scenario will happen," it is "which holdings survive being wrong about which scenario happens," and hard bifurcation is the scenario most likely to expose concentrated, single-scenario bets.
This lesson closes the course's arc: from understanding how the postwar trading system was built, through why it broke, to how to actually position for genuine uncertainty about what replaces it.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice, a geopolitical forecast, or a recommendation regarding any security, sector or country allocation. Scenarios are illustrative planning tools, not predictions, and probabilities are described qualitatively rather than precisely because no reliable quantitative basis for them exists. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
